title: parseGenbank and writeGenbank throw RangeError once a record has about 125k warnings or header lines (array spread into push)
description:
`parseGenbank` promises "Never throws", but several call sites spread an unbounded array into one function call. V8 caps call arguments at about 125k: inside Vitest 100,000 works and 125,000 throws.

Reader sites:
- `genbank.ts:162` `warnings.push(...recordWarnings)`
- `genbank-header.ts:225` `header.extraHeaderLines.push(...block.lines)`

Writer sites:
- `genbank-header.ts:323`, `genbank-header.ts:326-335` and `genbank-header.ts:339` (`out.push(...commentBlock(comment))`)
- `genbank.ts:373` `out.push(...formatHeader(record))`
- `genbank-features.ts:404`

Because of the writer sites, `writeGenbank` can throw on a record that `parseGenbank` itself returned.

Realistic trigger: a genome of 7.5 Mb or more (e.g. Streptomyces, any eukaryotic chromosome) whose ORIGIN keyword line is missing. This is the same class of malformed input the spec asks the reader to tolerate. Depending on which header block comes last, every sequence line becomes one of:
- a feature with an invalid location, one warning per line: reader throws at `:162`;
- a continuation of a REFERENCE block: reader throws at `genbank-header.ts:225`;
- a COMMENT continuation: reading works, the writer throws at `genbank-header.ts:339`.

Below the threshold the API is still unfriendly to a UI. The real 4.6 Mb E. coli fixture with only its ORIGIN line deleted gives 77,362 warnings (13.6 MB of text) and no cap or aggregation.

Fix: replace the spreads with a loop push, `concat`, or index assignment.
expected: `parseGenbank` returns best-effort records plus warnings, and never throws. `writeGenbank` can write any record `parseGenbank` produced.
actual:
Each case throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`:
- F1a at `parseGenbank` (`genbank.ts:162:14`)
- F1c at `readHeader` (`genbank-header.ts:225:38`)
- F1b at `formatHeader` (`genbank-header.ts:339:50`), called from `writeGenbank` (`genbank.ts:373`)

For the 4.6 Mb E. coli file without its ORIGIN line, `parseGenbank` does not throw but returns 77,362 warnings.

title: Multi-line feature locations are assembled in quadratic time (`location.endsWith` on a growing string)
description:
`buildRawFeature` (`genbank-features.ts:111-113`) runs `location.endsWith(',')` on every continuation line, right after `location += next`. V8 flattens the growing cons-string on each `endsWith`, so assembling a location written over N lines costs O(N × length). That breaks the spec's explicit rule "Avoid quadratic string building".

Micro-benchmark of the pattern alone: 20,000 appends take 3.0 s with `endsWith`, 2 ms without.

Measured through `parseGenbank`, compared with `parseLocation` on the same text:

| location lines | parts | `parseGenbank` | `parseLocation` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2,448 | 10,000 | 19 ms | 13–45 ms |
| 5,781 | 20,000 | 208 ms | 13–45 ms |
| 12,448 | 40,000 | 962 ms | 13–45 ms |
| 25,781 | 80,000 (2.76 MB file) | 3.9 s | 43 ms |

Each doubling multiplies the time by about 4.1×. Note that 3.9 s is already over the 3 s budget the spec sets for the 11.7 MB genome, here for a 2.76 MB file.

The implementer's "20,000-part join parsed in linear time" test calls `parseLocation` directly and bypasses the feature-table reader, so it misses this. E. coli is unaffected because its locations are short. Large joins and order()s, and hostile files, hit it.

Fix: test the last appended line (`next.endsWith(',')`), or collect the pieces in an array and join once.
expected: Parsing a feature whose location spans many lines takes time linear in the file size, comparable to `parseLocation` on the same text (about 45 ms here).
actual: `parseGenbank` takes 3,879 ms, against 43 ms for `parseLocation` on the same location text, and the test fails with `expected 3878.6 to be less than 1000`. Time grows about 4× per doubling of the join size.

title: FASTA: a BOM before a later '>' header (concatenated files) merges that header into the previous record and turns DNA into protein
description:
`parseFasta` strips a UTF-8 BOM only at the very start of the text (`fasta.ts:52`). A later header line `﻿>name` fails `line.startsWith('>')` (`fasta.ts:61`). Since JS `\s` matches U+FEFF, `line.replace(/[\s\d]+/g, '')` (`fasta.ts:66`) then turns the header into residues (`>name...`) and appends them to the previous record's sequence.

The header's letters include protein-only codes (E, F, I, L, P, Q...), so `detectMolecule` reclassifies the DNA record as protein, and the second record disappears. The only warning is "invalid character(s) replaced by X". Nothing reports the lost record or the flipped molecule type, and every downstream analysis (enzymes, ORFs, primers) then treats the plasmid as a protein.

Typical cause: FASTA files saved with a UTF-8 BOM (e.g. by Windows Notepad), concatenated with `cat a.fa b.fa` or `copy /b`, then decoded with `TextDecoder`, which strips only the leading BOM, as a Tauri webview does. Biopython 1.88 does not split the records either, but it does no molecule detection.

Fix: strip a leading U+FEFF from every line, or recognise `/^﻿?>/` as a header.
expected:
Two DNA records:
- `pUC19_fragment` with sequence `ACGTACGTACGTACGTACGT`
- `pET28_fragment` with description `sequence` and sequence `GGGGCCCCAAAATTTT`
actual:
One record: `{name: 'pUC19_fragment', molecule: 'protein', seq: 'ACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTXPETXFRAGMENTSEQUENCEGGGGCCCCAAAATTTT'}`.

The only warning is `invalid character(s) replaced by X: ">" (1), "_" (1)` (line 3).

title: FASTA header regex TOPOLOGY_MODIFIER is quadratic on long whitespace runs (ReDoS hang)
description:
`TOPOLOGY_MODIFIER = /\s*\[\s*topology\s*=\s*(circular|linear)\s*\]/gi` (`fasta.ts:23`) is unanchored and starts with `\s*`. For a header containing a run of n blanks or tabs not followed by `[`, the engine rescans the rest of the run from every start position, so the cost is O(n²).

Measured on one header line:
- 10k blanks: 31 ms
- 20k blanks: 119 ms
- 40k blanks: 444 ms
- 100k blanks: 2.4 s (100k tabs: 2.9 s)

A 1 MB header would block the UI or worker for minutes. Only hostile or corrupted files trigger it, so the severity is minor. No other regex in the module showed super-linear behaviour: LOCUS tokens, feature locations and `parseLocation` were tested up to 200k characters and finished in 0–2 ms.

Fix: drop the leading `\s*` (match `\[\s*topology...\]`) and collapse whitespace afterwards.
expected: The header is parsed in linear time: a few milliseconds for 100 kB.
actual: 2,472 ms for a 100 kB blank run (`expected 2472.49 to be less than 500`), growing quadratically: 31, 119 and 444 ms for 10k, 20k and 40k blanks.

title: GenBank: a BOM before a later LOCUS line (concatenated exports) drops that whole record
description:
`splitLines` removes a UTF-8 BOM only at the start of the text (`genbank.ts:67`), and `LOCUS_LINE = /^LOCUS(?:\s|$)/` (`genbank.ts:77`) does not match `﻿LOCUS`. After `cat a.gb b.gb` of BOM-prefixed exports, decoded with `TextDecoder` (which strips only the leading BOM), the second record is skipped. In the reproduction that is pBR322 with all its features.

The only signal is "472 line(s) outside any LOCUS ... // record were ignored", which says neither that a record was lost nor why. Biopython 1.88 also loses it (with `utf-8-sig` it reads only the first record). However, the spec lists a UTF-8 BOM among the artefacts the reader must accept, and this reader is otherwise deliberately more lenient than Biopython.

Fix: strip U+FEFF at the start of every line in `splitLines`, or allow `^﻿?LOCUS`.
expected: Two records, `SYNPUC19V` and `SYNPBR322`, or at least a warning explaining that a LOCUS line preceded by a BOM was skipped.
actual: Records: `['SYNPUC19V']` only. Warnings: `[{message: '472 line(s) outside any LOCUS ... // record were ignored', line: 104}]`.

title: Inner fuzzy markers merged away at the origin are dropped without the documented warning
description:
`parseLocation` documents that fuzzy markers on inner boundaries of a multi-part location are dropped *with a warning*. The check that emits that warning (`location.ts:528-534`) runs after `mergeOriginCrossings` (`location.ts:420-441`). When the merge joins `...L` and `1...` into one wrapping piece, it keeps only `prev.leftPartial` and `p.rightPartial`, so the inner `>` and `<` disappear before the check can see them.

Result: `join(51..>60,<1..10)` on a circular 60 bp record returns one segment `{50,70}` with no partial flags and an empty `warnings` array. The equivalent non-merging case `join(41..>50,<51..60)` does warn. Biopython 1.88 keeps both markers (`AfterPosition` and `BeforePosition` on the inner boundaries). This is a silent loss of annotation information, against the project rule to prefer explicit warnings.

Fix: test the inner partial flags before or while merging, and emit the same warning.
expected: The merged case also reports `fuzzy boundary inside a multi-part location cannot be stored and was ignored`, like the non-merging case.
actual: `{"ok":true,"strand":1,"segments":[{"start":50,"end":70}],"partialStart":false,"partialEnd":false,"warnings":[]}`. The test fails with `expected 0 to be greater than 0`.

title: parseGenbank throws a RangeError (it must never throw) when one record produces more than about 125,000 warnings; writeGenbank has the same flaw
description:
parseGenbank collects each record's warnings in `recordWarnings` and then appends them with a spread: `warnings.push(...recordWarnings)` (genbank.ts:162). When a single record has more than about 125,000 warnings, this exceeds V8's argument limit (Node 22.23). The call throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` and the caller gets no records and no warnings. This breaks the spec rule "Never throw on malformed input" and contradicts the report's claim that "the parser never throws".

A realistic trigger: a chromosome-scale annotated GenBank file whose ORIGIN was cut off (a truncated download). The feature table comes before ORIGIN, so it survives intact, and every feature beyond the cut produces a warning. The limit depends on the JavaScript engine.

The writer has the same pattern at genbank.ts:373 `out.push(...formatHeader(record))`, genbank-features.ts:404 `lines.push(...formatQualifier(...))` and genbank-header.ts:225. I also reproduced writeGenbank throwing the same RangeError for a 150,000-line COMMENT and for an 8 MB /note.

Fix: append in a loop (`for (const w of recordWarnings) warnings.push(w)`) or use concat.
expected: parseGenbank returns the record together with 150,000 'feature skipped' warnings and never throws. writeGenbank should not throw for large inputs either.
actual: RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded, thrown from `warnings.push(...recordWarnings)` (genbank.ts:162). Nothing is returned.

title: Reading a location that spans many lines takes quadratic time (the spec says to avoid quadratic string building)
description:
`buildRawFeature` builds a multi-line location with `location += next` and checks `location.endsWith(',')` on every line (genbank-features.ts:111-113). In V8, calling `endsWith` on the growing concatenated string flattens (copies) the whole string each time, so reading a location that spans n lines costs O(n²).

Measured times for `readFeatureTable` alone, on joins written by writeGenbank:

| Join parts | Lines | readFeatureTable | parseLocation on the same text |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10,000 | 4,126 | 10 ms | 8 ms |
| 20,000 | 9,126 | 204 ms | 11 ms |
| 40,000 | 19,126 | 952 ms | 22 ms |
| 80,000 | 39,126 | 3,915 ms | 31 ms |

parseLocation itself is linear. A standalone microbenchmark of `s.endsWith(',') ; s += line` shows the same pattern: 10k lines 568 ms, 20k 2.3 s, 40k 9.1 s.

The E. coli target is still met (about 0.16 s), so only very large joins are affected. The implementer's '20,000-part join in linear time' test calls parseLocation directly, so it never exercises the line accumulation.

Fix: track whether the last line ended with ',' (`next.endsWith(',')`) and collect the lines in an array, joining once at the end.
expected: Parse time grows linearly with location length: well under 1 s for an 80,000-part join (parseLocation needs 31 ms).
actual: 4.25 s. Time roughly quadruples each time the join size doubles (204 ms, then 952 ms, then 3,915 ms in readFeatureTable).

title: On circular records, '<' or '>' at the origin junction of a join are dropped silently, without the documented warning
description:
The parseLocation doc comment (lines 460-461) and the implementer's report both say inner '<' or '>' markers of a multi-part location "are dropped with a warning". On circular records this is not true.

The origin pieces are merged first by `mergeOriginCrossings` (location.ts:420-443, called at line 526). That merge keeps only `prev.leftPartial` and `p.rightPartial`. The inner-fuzzy check runs afterwards (lines 528-534), so the `>L` / `<1` flags are already gone when it looks.

Result: `join(91..>100,<1..10)` and `complement(join(91..>100,<1..10))` on a 100 bp circular record become one segment {90,110} with no partial flags and zero warnings. writeGenbank then writes `join(91..100,1..10)`, silently turning the uncertain boundaries into exact ones. The linear analogue `join(1..>10,<20..30)` does warn: "fuzzy boundary inside a multi-part location cannot be stored and was ignored". I confirmed the same behaviour through parseGenbank on full files.

Fix: check prev.rightPartial / p.leftPartial inside the merge, or run the inner-fuzzy check before merging.
expected: A warning such as 'fuzzy boundary inside a multi-part location cannot be stored and was ignored', as on linear records and as documented.
actual: No warning. Segments [{start:90,end:110}] with no partial flags. The rewritten location has exact boundaries.

title: '>a..b' and 'a..<b' are silently rewritten with the opposite uncertainty direction ('<a..b', 'a..>b')
description:
INSDC Feature Table 3.4.2.1 says '<' and '>' "may be used with the starting and ending base numbers to indicate that an end point is beyond the specified base number", so the symbol gives the direction. `range()` maps any marker to the same boolean: `leftFuzzy: start.marker !== null`, `rightFuzzy: end.marker !== null` (location.ts:248-249). `formatSpan` (line 551) always writes '<' on the left and '>' on the right.

So `>5..10` (start lies after base 5) is read as partialStart and written back as `<5..10` (start lies before base 5). Likewise `1..<9` becomes `1..>9`, and `complement(>3..12)` becomes `complement(<3..12)`.

No warning is produced. This is unlike every other approximation in this parser (one-of, within, inner fuzzies), and against the review rule to prefer explicit warnings over guessing. Biopython 1.88 keeps AfterPosition/BeforePosition and writes `>5..10` and `1..<9` back unchanged (checked with the oracle venv).

This is distinct from the documented 'partialStart means < on the left whatever the strand' limitation: here the written direction is inverted, not just mapped to a side. No fixture contains this form, so it is rare. Fix: warn when the marker points the 'wrong' way.
expected: Either keep the marker direction (Biopython writes '>5..10' and '1..<9' back) or emit a warning that the direction was changed.
actual: '>5..10' becomes '<5..10' and '1..<9' becomes '1..>9', with zero warnings at read time.

title: parseLocation wraps a span ending after base L on a circular record instead of clamping or dropping it, contradicting the spec and its own TSDoc
description:
In resolveSpan (location.ts lines 405-412), when end > L on a CIRCULAR molecule the reader keeps end > L and warns "read as running over the origin". The span therefore covers bases 1..(b-L) on the other side of the origin.

This contradicts two sources:
- The spec: "Positions beyond the sequence -> warning and clamp or drop, never crash".
- parseLocation's own TSDoc: "Positions before base 1 or after base L are clamped (the feature is then marked partial on that side) or, when a part lies entirely outside the sequence, that part is dropped".

A linear record clamps the same text (90..>100, partial end).

Where it bites: circular records whose coordinates run past the actual sequence, such as a truncated file or one whose LOCUS length is larger than its ORIGIN. The feature silently gains unrelated bases from the start of the molecule (with a wrap warning, but the stored feature is changed), so its featureSequence is wrong.

Biopython 1.88 keeps the feature as [89:120] and extracts only the 11 existing bases (CGGGGGGGGGG); clamping would give the same 11 bases. HHereditas instead returns 31 bases, the last 20 of which (A x 20) come from bases 1-20.

Suggested fix: on circular records, clamp end to L and set partialEnd, as the TSDoc says. Origin-spanning features are written as join(s..L,1..e) or s..e with s > e, and both forms are already merged correctly.
expected: parseLocation('90..120', 100, 'circular') gives segments [{start: 89, end: 100}] with partialEnd true, or the part is dropped. In both cases a warning is emitted. The feature in the truncated circular record has the sequence CGGGGGGGGGG (11 bases), as Biopython extracts.
actual: parseLocation gives segments [{start: 89, end: 120}], partialEnd false, with the warning "'90..120' ends after base 100: read as running over the origin of the circular molecule". The parsed feature's featureSequence is CGGGGGGGGGGAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA (31 bases): the 11 real bases plus bases 1-20 from the other side of the origin. Both tests fail with: expected [ { start: 89, end: 120 } ] to deeply equal [ { start: 89, end: 100 } ], and expected 'CGGGGGGGGGGAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA' to be 'CGGGGGGGGGG'.

title: One unindented line inside FEATURES silently drops every later feature
description:
In readRecord (lines 213-217) the feature table is the run of lines after FEATURES that start with an ASCII blank. The first line that does not start with a blank ends the table. The post-table loop (lines 238-244) then warns `unexpected line '<text>' ignored` and silently skips every following indented line, which is the entire rest of the feature table. The warning says that one line was ignored, not that features were dropped, so the UI cannot explain the loss.

Measured on new inputs:
- **Mutation fuzzing (seeded, 1380 fixture mutants parsed by Biopython 1.88):** all 71 mutants that lost features came from a single stray unindented line. No other mutation lost more than one feature.
- **pBR322_J01749.gb with one 'x' line inserted:** we keep 1 feature; Biopython keeps all 50 and only warns `line too short to contain a feature: 'x'`.
- **Raw newline inside a quoted /note (likely exporter bug):** a continuation line written at column 1, e.g. `/note="long note` followed by `broken here"`, also drops every later feature. Biopython rejects that file with a ValueError.
- **Related:** a FEATURES header with one leading blank drops all 50 pBR322 features with only `misplaced FEATURES line in the header ignored`. Biopython also loses them in that case.

The spec asks for best-effort records and accepts slightly wrong indentation.
expected: Every feature is kept, as Biopython does: abc, def and ghi in F1; 50 features in F1b. At most the stray line is ignored, with a warning.
actual: F1 keeps only ['abc']; the only warning is {message: "unexpected line 'stray text' ignored", line: 5}. F1b keeps 1 of 50 features ("expected [...] to have a length of 50 but got 1").

title: CONTIG records lose the CONTIG line and the N placeholder is written as real sequence (151 KB file becomes 315 MB)
description:
For a record with no ORIGIN data, readRecord (lines 261-274) fills the sequence with N up to the LOCUS length. The CONTIG line is never stored: it is not in meta.extraHeaderLines or meta.extras. Nothing in the returned record marks the sequence as a placeholder; only a free-text warning does. writeGenbank (line 406, formatOrigin) then writes the placeholder as a real ORIGIN block.

Consequences:
- **Fixture DS830848.gb (3,973 bytes, CON division):** written back as 5,599 bytes with 1,311 'n'. The `CONTIG      join(ABJB010667125.1:1..1311)` line is gone, and re-reading the written file gives no warning at all, so the placeholder has become indistinguishable from real sequence.
- **Chromosome-scale CON file (built for this review: LOCUS 248,956,422 bp, 2,000 gene features, CONTIG line, 151 KB):** parses in 21 ms, but writeGenbank takes 4.1 s and returns 315,495,836 characters of mostly 'n', without the CONTIG line. NCBI serves chromosome and scaffold entries in this CON form.
- **Biopython 1.88:** keeps annotations['contig'] and writes the CONTIG line with no ORIGIN (InsdcIO._write_sequence: "there is no need to record a long sequence of NNNNNNN...NNN").

The implementer's report lists the read-time placeholder but not this loss on write. The spec's round-trip goal is lossless GenBank output.
expected: Like Biopython: the CONTIG line is preserved (e.g. in meta) and written back, with no ORIGIN of N. At minimum the record carries a machine-readable placeholder marker, so writers and analyses do not treat L 'N' as real data.
actual: The written text has no CONTIG line and an ORIGIN of 1311 'n' (the first assertion fails: expected 'LOCUS       DS830848 …' to contain 'CONTIG      join(ABJB010667125.1:1..1311)'). Re-parsing the output returns warnings [] and seq 'NNNN…'. The chromosome-scale case writes 315 MB in 4.1 s.

title: ORGANISM indented by 4 blanks is silently merged into SOURCE (organism and taxonomy lost)
description:
headerKeyword (line 54) recognises a sub-keyword only with at most 3 leading blanks (`/^ {0,3}([A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*)(?=\s|$)/`). An ORGANISM line indented by 4 or more blanks therefore becomes a continuation line of SOURCE. SOURCE then contains the organism and the whole lineage, meta.organism and the taxonomy are lost, and no warning is emitted.

Biopython 1.88 takes the keyword as line[:12].strip(), so it reads source, organism and taxonomy correctly from the same text. The spec requires accepting slightly wrong indentation. For other sub-keywords (AUTHORS, TITLE, ...) the lines are only kept verbatim, so ORGANISM is the one modelled sub-keyword affected.
expected: source 'Escherichia coli', organism 'Escherichia coli', taxonomy 'Bacteria; Pseudomonadota; Gammaproteobacteria.' (as Biopython reads it), or at least a warning.
actual: meta.source = 'Escherichia coli ORGANISM Escherichia coli Bacteria; Pseudomonadota; Gammaproteobacteria.', meta.organism and the taxonomy are undefined, and warnings is [].

title: parseLocation/formatLocation return NaN coordinates for a NaN or undefined seqLength
description:
Both functions try to sanitise the length with `const L = Math.max(0, Math.floor(seqLength))` (lines 540 and 632). Math.max(0, NaN) is NaN, and Math.floor(undefined) is NaN too, so a missing or non-finite length passes through unchecked.

parseLocation then returns ok:true with a segment whose end is NaN, plus a warning that prints 'NaN'. On circular records it returns the NaN segment with no warning at all. formatLocation returns the text 'complement(NaN..NaN)'. A UI caller passing `record?.seq.length` while no record is loaded hits this. The NaN segment would then flow into features and be written into GenBank files.
expected: parseLocation returns { ok: false, error } (or finite, clamped segments). formatLocation never emits 'NaN'.
actual: parseLocation('20..5', NaN, 'linear') returns {ok:true, segments:[{start:19,end:NaN},{start:0,end:5}], warnings:["'20..5': start after end on a linear molecule, interpreted as join(20..NaN,1..5)"]}; the result is the same for seqLength undefined. With 'circular' it returns [{start:19,end:NaN}] and no warnings. formatLocation(..., NaN, 'linear') returns 'complement(NaN..NaN)'.

title: /translation wrapping splits an escaped "" pair, so the value's quote is doubled on re-read
description:
formatQualifier wraps /translation with wrapQualifierText(..., breakAnywhere = true) (lines 321-325), which cuts the text every 58 characters regardless of quote escaping. When a cut falls between the two quotes of an escaped `""` pair, the first line ends with `"` and has an even quote count.

Both our reader and Biopython then close the value at that line and append the next line as an unquoted continuation. The value read back contains two quotes instead of one, and each further round trip doubles it again.

Our own reader produces such values from malformed files. Mutation fuzzing found one: EU851978.gbk with its closing /translation line duplicated parses to a value containing `"`. So parse → write → parse is not a fixed point for that input. Biopython reads the written file the same wrong way (MMM…""KKK…).
expected: The value read back is 'M'×43 + '"' + 'K'×10: the writer never ends a line inside an escaped "" pair.
actual: The writer emits `/translation="MMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMM"` followed by the line `"KKKKKKKKKK"`. Read back, the value is 'M'×43 + '""' + 'K'×10 (plus a 'double quote ... not escaped' warning); Biopython 1.88 reads the same doubled quote.
